e.etymology: Used mainly in Latino families, where it is read as Spanish mar bella, beautiful sea, and matches Marbella, the resort city on Spain's Costa del Sol. It also echoes Maribel and Marisol.

assoc.t: Marbella, resort city on Spain's Costa del Sol

e.etymology: A modern American name, a variant of Amari with the E- of Emery and Emani. It has no separate meaning of its own.
The Portuguese form of John, written João, from Latin Iohannes and Hebrew Yochanan, God is gracious. US birth records drop the tilde.
e.note: Said roughly zhoo-OW with a nasal ending; English speakers often stumble over the spelling.

e.etymology: Best known as the short form of Huckleberry, from Mark Twain's Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (1884). Huck is also an old English surname from a medieval personal name later linked with Hugh.
namesakes: Huck Finn (runaway hero of Mark Twain's Adventures of Huckleberry Finn)

assoc.t: Huck Finn, Mark Twain's river-rafting boy hero

e.etymology: From the English word for the bird, Old English dufe, long a symbol of peace and of the Holy Spirit. It was used for girls in the late 1800s and has returned with other bird names.
namesakes: Dove Cameron (actress and singer of Disney's Descendants)

assoc.t: Dove, Unilever's soap and personal care brand

e.note: Shares its name with the Dove soap and Dove chocolate brands.

e.meaning: from an Irish surname: sweetheart, or little blackbird
e.etymology: A respelling of Lennon, an Irish surname from Ó Leannáin, linked to leannán, sweetheart, or from Ó Lonáin, from lon, blackbird. Parents usually choose Lennon for Beatle John Lennon.

assoc.t: John Lennon of the Beatles (spelled Lennon)

e.note: Sounds like both Lennon and Lenin, and the -yn spelling will need spelling out.

e.etymology: A spelling of Jalen or Jaylen, a name coined in 1973 for basketball player Jalen Rose from the names James and Leonard, and widely respelled since his 1990s fame.
A spelling used for more than one name: the Hebrew Ilana, tree, common in Jewish families, and a form of Elena or Alana.
A spelling of Kaylyn, a 20th-century American combination of Kay and Lynn that also sits close to Kayla and Caitlin.
A modern American name in the family of Mariyah, Aniyah and Saniyah, built on the popular -iyah ending. It has no settled meaning.
A Yiddish pet name used in Hasidic communities for Yehudis (Judith) and Yitta. Judith is Hebrew Yehudit, woman of Judea.
A modern Indian name usually glossed as unique, from Sanskrit a-, not, and dvi, two: one without a second.
Best known from Revan, the Jedi turned Sith Lord of the 2003 Star Wars game Knights of the Old Republic. It also fits the sound of Evan, Devin and Raven.

assoc.t: Darth Revan of Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic

e.etymology: A spelling of Cataleya, from the cattleya orchid, a genus named for English horticulturist William Cattley. The name took off after Zoe Saldana played Cataleya in the 2011 film Colombiana.
The Latin and Spanish form of Margaret, from Greek margarites, pearl. In Spanish, margarita is also the word for a daisy.

assoc.t: margarita, the tequila and lime cocktail

e.note: In the US, most people think first of the cocktail.

e.etymology: The French form of Dionysius, devoted to Dionysus, the Greek god of wine. Saint Denis, a 3rd-century bishop of Paris, is a patron of France; in English it is the British and Irish spelling of Dennis.
namesakes: Denis Leary (comedian and star of Rescue Me)
Denis Villeneuve (director of Dune and Arrival)

e.etymology: From the Yiddish name Kaila; in modern use it is mostly a spelling of Kayla, sometimes of Kyla. In Hawaiian, kaila is a word for style, borrowed from English.
A respelling of Ryan, from the Irish surname Ó Riain, descendant of Rian, a name usually explained as little king. The Rh- spelling is used mostly for girls.
From Arabic hadi, a guide, from the verb hada, to lead aright. Al-Hadi, the Guide, is one of the names of God in Islam.
From an American surname of German origin, Rüger, a Germanic name built from words for fame and spear. As a given name it follows the firearms maker Ruger, like Remington and Colt.
e.note: Most Americans know Ruger as a gun brand.

e.etymology: A spelling of Lainey, a pet form of Elaine, the Old French form of Helen, also linked to the surname Lane. Lainey has risen fast in the 2020s alongside country singer Lainey Wilson.

e.meaning: save us, we pray; a shout of praise
e.etymology: From the Hebrew plea hoshia na, save us, we pray, which became a shout of praise. Crowds cry Hosanna as Jesus enters Jerusalem, and the word is sung in churches on Palm Sunday.

e.meaning: settlement on the River Glyme, or hill town
e.etymology: From an English surname taken from places such as Glympton, settlement on the River Glyme, and Glinton. It has been a given name since the 19th century and gives the short form Clint.
namesakes: Clint Eastwood (actor and director, born Clinton Eastwood Jr.)
Clinton Kelly (co-host of What Not to Wear)

assoc.t: Bill and Hillary Clinton, former president and first lady

e.note: Most Americans will think first of Bill and Hillary Clinton.

e.etymology: A variant of Alvin, from Old English names such as Aelfwine, elf friend. It is also common in Azerbaijan, Turkey and the Balkans.
namesakes: Elvin Jones (jazz drummer in John Coltrane's quartet)
Elvin Hayes (Hall of Fame NBA forward)

e.meaning: man of the people, or lion man
e.etymology: From Greek Leandros, built on aner, man, with either leos, people, or leon, lion. In Greek myth Leander swam the Hellespont each night to reach his lover Hero.
namesakes: Leander (lover of Hero in Greek myth)

e.etymology: A spelling of Miley, popularized by singer Miley Cyrus, whose childhood nickname came from Smiley. It can also be read as My- plus Lee, like Kylee and Rylee.

e.meaning: sea (when a spelling of Hawaiian Kai)
e.etymology: The Welsh form of Kay, as in Sir Kay (Cai) of Arthurian legend, probably from the Roman name Caius. In the US it is mostly a spelling of Kai, Hawaiian for sea. Cai is also a Chinese surname.
From the English title for a woman who rules an empire or is married to an emperor, from Old French emperesse and Latin imperator, commander. It joins title names such as Royal, Reign and Queen.
A modern American name with no settled origin, close in sound to Zia, Zaya and Mya.
A pet form of Robert, especially popular in Scotland, and of Roberta. Robert comes from a Germanic name meaning bright fame, brought to England by the Normans.
namesakes: Robbie Robertson (guitarist and songwriter of The Band)

e.etymology: The Spanish form of Reynold, from a Germanic name built from ragin, counsel, and wald, rule. Reinaldo is the other common spelling.
From the English word for moderation, from Latin temperantia. Puritans used it as a virtue name from the 16th century, and it revived in the 2000s with Dr. Temperance Brennan of the TV series Bones.
namesakes: Temperance Brennan (forensic anthropologist of the TV series Bones)

assoc.t: Dr. Temperance Brennan of the TV series Bones
temperance movement, the campaign against alcohol
